newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end mostly lower after 3-yr sale.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end mostly lower after 3-yr sale.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended a bit lower on Tuesday but were little fazed by soggy demand in the three-year note auction.
"It doesn't look like the market had much of a reaction, but overall the auction was fairly poor," said Greg Carr, bond market analyst at A.G. Edwards and Sons Inc.

The average yield on the Treasury's sale of three-year paper was in line with expectations at 6.44 percent but analysts said demand was disappointing and may have been dampened by the run up in prices last week.

The auction had a one-basis-point tail and the Treasury said bids covered the amount sold by a comparatively low 2.08 times. The average bid-to-cover ratio for the last five three-year auctions was 2.3.

"Interest wasn't that deep," said Carr. "So, for the amount of funds that were available, it looks as though the marketplace has kind of backed off since the yield levels have come down dramatically from last week."
Analysts said the results suggest current prices would only look like a bargain if they assumed the Federal Reserve did not have another interest rate hike up its sleeve.
The market is looking for clues from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan when he speaks in New York on the evening of Thursday May 8.
Analysts said the market seems about evenly divided on whether Fed policy makers will hike rates again on May 20.

"We're sitting at about 50/50, maybe slightly tilted towards a hike," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc. "The real thing is people assume that is going to be the last one for some time ... I would say Greenspan himself throwing cold water on that notion is maybe the biggest risk."

Trade was very subdued in advance of the first leg of the refunding, which concludes on Wednesday with the sale of $12 billion in 10-year notes. The next tranche should produce a better result, analysts said.
"I would expect the 10-year to go well. Then we'll see how the distribution goes. There's always a chance for a problem," Youngdahl said.
U.S. March factory orders, which dropped 1.6 percent on Tuesday, and inventories which rose 0.2 percent, were in line with forecasts and had little impact on the market.
Some selling by hedge funds of two- and five-year issues was reported and weighed on the market early in the session.
But unwinding of curve flattening trades in the run up to the auction may have propped up the near end, experts said.

"Maybe somebody was covering a flattening trade where they were short three-year notes and long 10-year notes and decided: 'hey maybe I can get it cheaper by buying the three year in the auction'," said Larry Dyer, government strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"The only story is really just the yield curve story," he added.
The three-year note ended down 3/32 at 98-20/32 with a yield of 6.42. The benchmark 30-year bond closed down 4/32 at 96-22/32, with a yield of 6.89 percent.

In the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bills were four basis points lower at 5.04 percent and six-month bills were off one basis point at 5.34 percent. Year bill rates were up two basis points at 5.56 percent.

Two-year notes ended down 2/32 at 100-5/32, yielding 6.29 percent. Fives were down 4/32 at 100-9/32 and a yield of 6.56 percent and tens were down 4/32 at 97-1/32, yielding 6.67 percent. ((--212 859 1667))
